blocks.x: It looks like it's a coin, doesn't it? What's your right name, anyway?
Conrad Rodman Jones III.
The funny thing you don't look Jewish.
I don't look Rodman, is she?
Is that a Jewish name? I know so.

No, I don't think so. Conrad is, I think it was German, although it is spelled with a C. The Rodman is an old family name from back in the Civil War days when one of my relatives married an old Yankee Captain Rodman, and the Jones is Welsh.
And I made a joke about that because Howard Patterson is always just in that feud and being one, he's just a collector of town jokes. Let me check it. Okay, how do you spell Germanalan?
Capital R, little o-d-m-a-n.
Okay, you're Conrad Rodman Jones III with a capital T, we said by the way.
Is that how it is? Yeah.
And what's today's date?
I think it's the 2nd, but of what month, I'm not sure. August, probably.
Yeah, I thought it was the 3rd.
It could be. I have one of those calendar watches on, and if there was only 30 days in last month, the watch has 31 days on it, and I forgot to change it.
Yeah. You've got plenty to do today, huh?
Yeah, Monday. Yeah. It is Monday, yeah, that's right. Monday the 3rd.
Yeah, I think we've got back to work. It's August, 1981. How do you spell your son's name? D-E-N?
D-E-N-N-I-S, Dennis. Ah, I see.
And...
He's the Rodman too.
He's the Rodman too. And who's he named after? Dennis.
I don't know. Just a name that we liked. Oh, it looks good.
Yeah.
There was a little dissension because the family wanted us to carry on the tradition with the 4th, but figured enough was enough.
I swear. I don't think we're getting all that hum. Yeah, we are. We're getting the hum on the right channel again. I was worried there for a minute we're going to lose all of our hum. But...
They give it a realistic effect.
Yeah. Well, this equipment dates from 65, the tape machine, and the microphones are probably from 19...
...or before. 60, before, over 20.
These were aboard the Enola Gay.
No, not quite that bad. You interested in the war between Japan and the U.S.?
Oh, not necessarily.
You just happened to know that the Enola Gay dropped the atomic bomb.

I saw one of the planes that dropped the atomic bomb. I'm not sure if it... I think it was the Enola Gay at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base at the museum. It's on display there. Out in the parking lot. Where is that?
Outside of Dayton, Ohio.

Well, you got around Ohio, that's right. Yeah, with the Mac Stitt Band. We were working there at some short-lived jazz club called the New Farm Club. And on one of our days off, my wife and the kiddies and I packed up and went out to the Air Force Museum. Which has nothing to do with jazz, I understand.

Well, that has something to do with you and you have something to do with jazz. It's all part of the same story. Anyway, I was thinking about all these brass bands and things and I asked you about carnival berets like the Jefferson City Buzzards. You said you weren't around magazines, streets, nights, or...

No, I lived out in Lakeview. And I never heard too many of those marching bands. In fact, like I said, the only ones that I can remember hearing would be the funeral bands that passed around Cleveland Avenue where my father had his business in that neighborhood. You know, it was black around and they had a lot of... Well, the funerals would have the procession there to them in that neighborhood.
Now, you went to carnival parades sometimes. Would you come in to Canal Street, Canal Boulevard, Broad Street, or any place?

My daddy had a business there by the Young Hotel, which was on La Salle and Canal. And we were pretty much based around that. When we went to carnival parades, I would go down there. And at that time, as I remember it, Richard, the parades went down that far. And I think some of them used to turn in there on La Salle Street and head back up toward the river. To the best of my recollection. But I would watch from around there, because you had a bathroom to go to, you know.
Oh. Well, that's always a problem. I've waited for a long time. With kids, yeah. With adults, too. Especially when you follow something like the buses.

And in those days, I can remember, too, there wasn't... It didn't seem like there were quite as many people watching the parades. It was pretty much a local event. Now it's become a fad, the place to go. Yeah. It's uncomfortable at times.
What about Broad Street? Did you ever see anything on Broad Street?
No, not that I can recall.
Pete Fountain talks about that. I think he talks about Harold Peterson's store and how he'd be back in that neighborhood. And, uh, I just wanted, did you know him when you were quite young?

I met Mr. Peterson when I was about, um, I guess 16 years old. He had the little music shop there on Broad by Orleans. Mm-hmm. And, uh, a bunch of us kids would go over there all the time and talk to him. He was, he was, was, I'm speaking about him in the past tense. He was a wonderful man. And, uh, for some reason or another, he took a special interest in the kids. And it wasn't that we spent a whole lot of money in his shop. Mm-hmm. We just, uh, he just liked to see the kids play and was, uh, very helpful in any way that he could be to us. It was always a pleasure just to go over there and talk to him.
Yeah, he always struck me as that kind of man. Everybody's always said that. Who did you see in a shop when you were going there?

Oh, gee, you'd run into all kind of, uh, musicians. At that time, uh, well, we were kids and they, you know, weren't really on, on, uh, not that we weren't on speaking terms, but we weren't socially involved with the older musicians. Mm-hmm. They would come in, take care of their business and, uh, leave. Yeah. But mostly with, uh, just the kids that I grew up with and other young musicians in the area would go be in there, you know.
But people like George Girard and Pete Frattner with the Basin Street Six, were they older or younger?

They, they're older than I am. Pete's about three years older than I am. Mm-hmm. And George was about, oh, two or three years older than Pete. Mm-hmm. So they were, uh, they were grown men, see, when we were just kids. Yeah, you had that idea. Oh, yeah, they were, you know, untouchables.
And were their sonos that much older than you?

Well, Frank was about two years older than I was. Mm-hmm. Um, and Freddie was still, I think Freddie was maybe four or five years older than Frank. Uh, I'm not certain, I, uh, I, I got to know the Asuntos when I started working with the Basin Street Six, and I was, uh, about 19, and they were working down the street at the famous door. And we, you know, got to know each other again. The Asuntos and Betty and all of the, uh, the folks in Frank's band, they were much younger than most of the rest of the bands on Bourbon Street at that time. Yeah.
That gave you a special bond or not?
It probably did, yeah. Did you ever listen to Hank Williams, correct?
Sure. Hank Williams is one of my favorite songwriters and singers, oh, I love him, yes.
Yeah, well you've been to that your father like country western.
Uh, I can remember when the Grand Ole Opry used to come to New Orleans on a street.

They would perform in a municipal auditorium and I went once with a friend of the family's. And I met, uh, his last wife. They were married here. One of the ceremonies were here in the auditorium. I didn't go to the ceremony, but I met her at Tony Almarico's on the, uh, radio program, the radio station. But yeah, I loved Hank Williams.
Would Tony broadcast remote from the Parisian room or did you go to the station?

Tony had a five-day-a-week radio broadcast from the station that he played. He was a disc jockey. And then he had, gosh, it must have been about three broadcasts. Let's see, he had one on WWL and then he had, uh, one on WJMR, which was a station that he broadcast from, uh, disc jockey. And then he had a third one for the Armed Forces Network or something like that. So he did, spent the best part of his Sunday afternoons doing radio broadcasts, all from the Parisian room.

Yeah, well I can remember JMR and I would go in there to see him. He did his own commercials and played records. That's right. And I'd lend him some of my records from time to time. Uh-huh. I was working for Mercury Records, you know. Or William B. Allen, who was the distributor. Uh-huh. I could sort of check those dates out sometime, but I imagine there was plenty of documentation. Do you have any brothers and sisters?

I have one brother who is, uh, seven years younger than I am. His name is Carl Jones. And he is a colonel in the United States Army, stationed in the Pentagon. Just about to retire. He's got about another year of service to go. And, uh, he'll be retiring at the ripe old age of about 40, full colonel's pay. And, uh, he has really no interest in music at all. He never did, uh, that I can remember, display any, uh, musical traits. He was a very, very intelligent boy, young man. And, uh, always did wonderfully in school. I think he majored in mathematics and Loyola. And, uh, went to the service, went through OCS, and has been there ever since.
Did you have a phonograph at home? I think I actually read it.

Uh-huh. Yeah, we sure did. And, uh, let's, I said we had, uh, some cowboy records. And, uh, as I'm thinking back on it, uh, yesterday, I remember discussing it with, uh, Glenn Wilson. A few novelty records, such as the Red Angle Joe Stafford things. Uh-huh. I'm sure you're familiar with it. Cigarettes and Horse Gain. No.
Temptation.
And, but it was all 78s. There were no LPs in those days.
So, you were pretty young then, before the LP era. You're talking about the 40s mainly then. Yeah. Maybe some of the 30s or something.

I can remember, uh, some of that, I don't know, birthday or something, Christmas, I got a very small phonograph, uh, that played 45 records only. And I must have been, that must have been maybe 1950 or somewhere around that. That was, they played at a slower speed. They played at 45s. Yeah.
And that was, uh, probably an RCA victim. It surely was.
Yeah. I, I'm trying to remember the, the, uh, I can't remember the songs. The first record that we had for it. For a long time it was the only one I had for it.

Well, sure. And, uh, well, they were competing with the Columbia in the 33 and it was a battle. And it was a battle that I can, well, I was in the music business and record business. And I guess there were a lot of things you couldn't get on 45. But you could get on LP and vice versa.
Mm-hmm. Yeah.
Yeah. Anyhow, uh, you said that you learned a lot of songs at home.
Mm-hmm.
What sort of songs would you sing? I'll play, I'll bowl.

Uh, it would be, uh, mostly, I can remember we did a lot of Irving, we had a lot of Irving Berlin sheet music. And, uh, things from Broadway shows. Mm-hmm. Uh, I can, I remember we had the sheet music for Cabin in the Sky. If I'm not mistaken, it had a picture of, uh, Ethel Waters on the front. This is a long time ago. Uh, and we had Irving Berlin's Remember. And we had Always. Uh-hmm. On sheet music. Oh, gee, I, we had stacks and stacks of it. Once again, Neil, like you said, if I had only known then, but some way or another, uh, they've all gotten away from us. Mm-hmm. Just, uh, been given away or thrown away over the years. Some of them, I wish I had them all right now, because I am back in the business of collecting music again.
You can, you can find a lot of those things.

You can, but let me tell you how much you'll pay for it. Mm-hmm. Through the nose. In, uh, outside of Decatur, Illinois, last year my wife and I went up, went out to this place way out in the country that sells antiques and junk with a Q, you know. Mm-hmm. And, uh, I came across a copy of Always, that incidentally is autographed. By Irving Berlin. Gee. And, uh, the guy opened up his heart and soul to me for four dollars. That seems cheap, but it's not a good thing. Yeah, I, I'm not sure he was aware that it was autographed. It was in a stack of music that was maybe three feet high. One of many stacks, yeah. Mm-hmm. But the, uh,
The score on rate was $2, $3, $4, depending on the condition of it.

Well, you ought to go see Bill Russell. Well, for example, he bought John Stark stock. And he doesn't know whether to sell it or not. People are getting ridiculous prices for a rate around New York. And Russell doesn't believe in the product system or something like that. He likes to sell things on the car.
Anyway. He should really stay in business a long time.
He sells things very cheap.
I went down and priced some stocks, stock arrangements. Things that used to go for a buck for the entire stock is now $18, $19.
I hope they were good stocks. Well, I don't want to get up on the subject of a rate and all that too much. I guess you did play some stocks. Oh, yeah.
No.
We better come to that later. Because I wanted to keep you on the subject of music at home. Did you play instrumental music ever at home? Are we always singing? Mostly singing or playing piano.

I'm trying to think. We had no other instruments at home other than the piano and that banjo. I didn't get my, I didn't play any other instrument or have any contact with any other instrument until I went to the military school. Yeah.
Did your great aunt play piano? Right. Anybody else in the family play it?

Not well enough to say anything about it. Everybody played a little bit. We all took lessons as a matter of course. I, as a kid, had a lot of other things I would have rather been doing than practicing my piano. Oh, yeah. And it didn't stick on me until much later.
Do you remember the first march you ever learned? How about you?

As a very little boy, my mother would take me to my grandmother's house. She had a wind up Vic Troller. And she had a bunch of march records. She would show me how to operate it. And I'd wind it up, crank it up, put the record on, and march around the room to probably Stars and Stripes Forever or one of those marches, by whom I don't know.
And would you play the banjo?
No. That was even before that, as a little, maybe three or four year old boy.
Oh, yeah. And did you play marches on the trumpet when you battled that?
When I first started playing, that was all I did play, because I was at a military school in the school band. And I learned how to play the instrument to play marches.
Yeah. And what did you play? Do you remember the marches there?

We did a lot of Susan marches. And there are some standard marches that even today, I notice that are very popular amongst high school bands. You'll hear them playing in a Rose Bowl parade or things like that, or see them in parades in the street. I don't remember the names of the book. We always refer to them by the color of the book. It was the red book or the blue book or the green book. And number, so and so march in the red book. I don't know. And they all had very common names and were fairly easy to play, very forgettable melody lines. And then we had some of the Susan marches that were very difficult for a 35 piece high school marching band to play, these grand arrangements.
But they were forgettable, you say? Most of the other ones, yeah.
Yes, they were. Yes, they were.
Do you remember the first song you learned how to play?

I can remember one of the first jazz songs I learned how to play was the 12th Street Rag. God, it was so hard. It was, it involves some really heavy fingering for me back in those days. But I practiced and practiced and practiced until I finally got to Dark Knight.
Did you read that at all? I didn't read it.

I didn't have the music for it. You didn't have the music for it. I did it all by ear. And then not too long after that I started learning songs and I would memorize all the choruses and I could sing to you each part of the Dixie Glan Band. I knew all the parts, the clarinet part, I could sing that to you, the trombone part, I could sing all of them to you and could eventually play them. I would memorize them and copy all the choruses, the clarinet chorus, the high society and all that. And I guess that was the way I learned how to eventually how to improvise.
What about, did you ever hear of Pee Wee Hunt?
Oh sure, yes.
Was he popular then?

Yeah, Pee Wee Hunt had a whole bunch of hit records back in what had to be, what, 1949, 50, somewhere? Yeah, 48. He had a pretty big record on High Society. Really? Yeah. And South, 12th Street Rag, a song called O, O-H.
Yeah. I think Tom Brown played or something like that.
Did he?
He made a record of it.
They were all very well done and I guess you could say even danceable most of them were for the dancing of that time.
Seems to me they were standard numbers to that.
They were, except for O. Not now. At least, I don't think it was standard. No. It may have been an old one that had been revived. It was an old one.

Was it? According to Tom. Mm-hmm. I can just remember that. It's something that Raymond Burke and Tom Brown and I discussed. I mean, Raymond told me that. Mm-hmm. Raymond is full of miscellaneous information that he picked up talking to Sidney Aaron and Tom Brown or somebody one time or another.

I can remember another. It was on the back of one of their records. It was a song called Bessie Couldn't Help It that was done, if I'm not mistaken, by Bing Crosby with the Paul Whiteman band. A little novelty, semi-novelty tune.
I know Big Spider-Bag went on.
Big Spider-Bag what? Recorded it.
Did he? Bessie Couldn't Help It with the Ogie Cominical but that's another story. We went to Big's last time, didn't we?
Briefly, yes.
Briefly, yeah. Anyway.

You know, now that I was thinking back on it, we were discussing what influence Bobby Hackett was on me. And I can remember now, every night on the radio, maybe 8 o'clock, 9 o'clock at night, I had to be in the late 40s again, 48, 49, or 50. They had an hour of recorded music, sentimental or ballads. And quite often they played the Jackie Gleason records with Bobby Hackett. The original Gleason Hackett things with songs like Alone Together and My Funny Valentine. And that is the first I remember hearing of Bobby Hackett. And I became aware of him as a player. And not too long after that, I got an album of Eddie Condon. And they had different bands on each record. It was the, you know, the 478 albums, the 10-inch records. And they had different players on each record. And on two of the sides were Lee Wiley. And one song she sang was The Man I Love. And I think the other one was Someone To Watch Over Me. And Bobby backed her up on it, as only Bobby could do. And then I believe he was on one, he did one called My One and Only, which was a George Gershman tune.
I don't think I ever owned that album.
It's available on 78.
I used to buy a lot of Condon records. Of course I used to hear Condon live on the record.
Yeah, see I only heard him once. Live. And that was at his club, the new club downtown. But I listened to his band whenever possible, you know, on records.
Oh yeah. Well, he was a great spokesman during that time.
Oh yes, he did an awful lot for the renaissance of that music. It was going through an upsurge in those days.
Yeah. Well, and we mentioned Paul Whiteman, but never did he get to that TV show very much. He just barely mentioned it last time I think. What happened with the TV show? How about that?

Let me see, let me put this together. When the junior band, Tony Amarico's, I forget the circumstances. If I'm not mistaken, we had done a couple of Nord TV shows. And TV was pretty hot stuff in those days. I think we only had one channel then, WDSU. And some kind of way or another, we were in some kind of a battle of the bands. And we were chosen to be the band to go to the Paul Whiteman show. Not as contestants. We did not go as contestants. Just as a feature. And we made the trip to Philadelphia by train. And we played in a parade, which in the Christmas season in Philadelphia is not the most pleasant time of the year to be playing outdoor parade. And did the television show at Town Hall. And then we went to New York and did a radio show. We had a weekly national radio show. And we played on that. And then it was back home by train. It was very, very exciting for 17, 16 year old boys to be. Actually, we were just on our own. We had no chaperones. We put on a train and got there. They met us at the train and took care of us after we got there. But we were alone on the train for about 24 hours. And it was really very thrilling. New Orleans is, was not the, well it was the big town as far as we concerned. But it really wasn't.
Were you scared? To death.
To death.
Radio and TV both scared you?

Television especially scared. Yeah. I was the, I think I was the oldest in the group. So I tried to be very cool about it. And what is the Peter Principle? Is that the Peter Principle? Something's going to happen. It will or something. And I can remember that it was a couple of last minute calamities. Now that's live television. No videotape. Yeah. I mean it was filmed. But it was, it was going out live at the time. And I think it was, it was Bruce Voorhees was late for the, we couldn't find him. And while they were doing the commercial they were supposed to be setting up and Bruce was nowhere to be found. And the Hare Breath Harry thing, the last moment comes walking up just in time to start playing the song. Of course anybody that knows Bruce knows that he's a character.
But didn't he ever bother to tune up?
I don't think that ever bothered him that much.
No I mean if you were there at the last minute. Did y'all bother to tune up when you were playing any music tonight?

Yeah I've, I've always been conscious of intonation. Probably, in fact I've probably been too conscious of it and it's always bothered me. Yeah. That's always been uppermost in my mind. Just being in tune.
You never felt good enough for jazz? No. I can remember hearing Bergen say that among many other people.
When it's good enough for jazz it should be in tune.
Yeah. Well different people, different actors.

That's true. If you're playing some very close harmony and it's out of tune it's going to sound pretty horrible. It's like listening to an out of tune piano. If you're doing unisons and everybody's out of tune and it's going to sound just like an old piano with none of the three strings in tune it's just going to sing at you. Yeah.

Well some people like it. Anyway, do you remember your first gig, what you call your first job? Yeah. I played a block party. Ah, jeez I'm trying to think of the neighborhood. Um, I had a lady, Evelyn Ravardica who owned a restaurant by my daddy's house, by my daddy's business.

And she hired the band to play this block party, which would be, I'm trying to think of which side is which. On Knaustra, you know where the Warren Easton side is. I'm trying to think of the block party. I'm trying to think of the block party. I'm trying to think of the neighborhood. Ah, jeez I'm trying to think of the neighborhood. I had a lady, Evelyn Ravardica who owned a restaurant by my daddy's house, by my daddy's business. And she hired the band to play this block party, which would be, I'm trying to think of which side is which. On Knaustra, you know where the Warren Easton side is.

on Warren Eastern High School, that side of Canal Street, but in a few blocks deeper, past Orleans, up around that neighborhood. I forget the name of the street, but it was in that area, up around there. But it would be...
This is not near the Jones.
No, no. This would be like...in fact, it was kind of like...this Miro Street, is that up around there? I think it was on Miro Street someplace.
Miro and Tom Tito right there.

Somewhere around there, if I'm not mistaken. But it was just the kids, and we played something like, I don't know, we might have gotten every bit of $25 for the whole job. And it was, we played, played, played, played. At that time we might have known ten tunes all together, the whole band, but we played and had a good time. The people danced and we thought we were terrific. And they probably did too. They had a good time. Sure.
That's $25 for the whole band. Oh yeah. I see. And how many pieces?
It could have been anywhere from six to seven or eight. At that time we would, sometimes if the guitar player was, couldn't make the job, we used the guitar player with the piano.
Sometimes we had neither. That wasn't easy, huh?

No. We used to go down and play at Buris, at Buck Jones's in Buris for I believe $35, covering transportation and everything on Saturday night. That was seven pieces too, a six piece band and a girl singer. Teresa Kelly was the girl singer. Were you familiar with Teresa? Another name somewhere. About seventh piece with Teresa Greer stuff. About seventh seventh That was seven pieces too, a six piece band and a girl singer. Teresa Kelly was the girl singer. You familiar with Teresa?
I know the names.
I think our ex-husband teaches here. Law school, couch.
Couch? Yes. I don't know. I think.
Either here or Loyola.

All right. Now, we're talking about that. Oh, this is the second reel of Connie Jones April. Yeah, August. Distracted trying to do too many things at once. Okay. We're talking about that band, the first band. Did it have a name?
Yes, that was the Dixie Cats.
The Dixie Cats.

The Dixie Cats, yes. Now, since those days, I must have seen 300 bands named Dixie Cats in different spellings. But every town has got a band named the Dixie Cats. In fact, there's one out in San Diego. Phillip Andrine and that bunch of bands. And that's the Dixie Cats with a K-A-T-Z. Dixie Cats. But that was something. We had a bass drum logo and everything. A tomcat in a zoot suit swinging a chain.
Ah.
Oh, it was, yeah, it was.
And it probably seemed like a very original idea, the whole thing, you'd call it the Dixie Cats. Yeah.
Yes, it did. Uh-huh.
I wonder if you had any inspiration.
I don't remember.
I would have automatically think of the Bobcats.
I would, too, yeah. That was the first thing that comes to mind. But if, and I had listened to the Bobcats a lot, so it may have had a big influence on it.
Well, you still listen to the Bobcats in mind, though.
Every chance I get.
I mean, you can't help it. I think about it when I go, say, to Parasol, St. Patrick's Day, or something like that. They all play more to the Bobcats.
That's got to be the unofficial theme of Mardi Gras, the March of Bobcats.
I'm not sure that people pay much attention to that. I don't get the publicity, but it's really true.

And I did an album a few years ago that did the March of the Bobcats on it. And I patterned the arrangement after the Crosby thing. So much so that you have to be very careful when you're listening to it until the solos. See, the solos are different. But I think it was Pepsi Cola used it as background music. Mardi Gras promotion here the last couple of years.
Who was the band leader?
Me.
And what company did you do that for?

For that jazz entrepreneur, whatever his name is, Albert St. Germain for the Maison Bourbon. That's the one with that memorable recording of Rick Nelson screaming, do you know what it means to Miss New Orleans? I'm so proud of.
And what does the color look like?

It's, let's see, that's the album The Yellow Dog Blues. And it's got this, it looks like some kindergarten guy drew a picture of the yellow dog sitting in the middle of, sitting by a train station in Mississippi. And what's the name of the city in Mississippi?
Well, Moorhead is the name of the real town.
Where the yellow dog crosses the southern.
Yeah.
And Morgan, Morgan, Mississippi, is it not?
Well, the real town is Moorhead.
Moorhead, okay.
But Jack Cooler, the artist, his old friend of mine, that's right.
He outdid himself on that. Somebody was misinformed. He outdid himself on that.

Yeah, and of course, his shop is in the same building where Leonard Kirk's lived, and Moorhead has to get him about that. You know, it's one of those small world things where he got all of his misinformation.
I just assumed I'd talk about that album. All right. Okay. That's the thing that will haunt me to my grave. It'll follow me to my grave.
Well, I bought the album, and then Harvey made me return it. Harvey moved to me and said, get the other one. So I'll get the other one if you return that.

It's funny. It's the same band. We did two albums within three weeks with the same band. And really, the Yellow Dog Blues album had some, a couple of good, some of my best arrangements were on the Yellow Dog Blues album. And they got thrown into the trash can. The tapes got sidetracked. So they would have enough time to put Miss New Orleans on it because of the, the guy says, oh, it'll sell more records with that song on it. And I think one of the songs that they threw away was Sensation Rag, which I guess is the best arrangement I ever did in my life. And I forget the other song. And it was basically the same band on both dates. But one was done at Cosmos, the George Buck album. And Cosmo just had a way with a Dixieland band, Cosmo Metasms. And it sounds like two different bands. The feeling was so much better at Cosmos and so much more relaxed. And it was not that the other studio did anything wrong because everything was right. But it's, again, we get back into the playing in tune. The piano was tuned probably too perfectly and isolated too much. And it was, it just does not have that, it just has too neat of a feeling. To make myself clear, everything is just too neat, almost computerized.

I've heard engineers tell the musicians that there wasn't enough separation. So they really isolated them like you're talking about. Did you ever have any problems with that on the audience? Where you couldn't hear the other members of the band?

I did an album in Philadelphia with the band I was with up there. And it was a rock and roll studio primarily. They did rock and roll dates. Knew nothing about setting up for a Dixieland band. So what he did was put the trombone player and myself in a booth and closed the door on us. We had no earphones. What we did is count it off and then we had to watch the drummer watch his stick to keep time. Because we couldn't hear what was going on. We could, when we weren't playing, we could hear what was going on. But when we were playing, our own sound filled up the booth and we couldn't hear what was happening. So we had to watch the drummer's hands to keep time. That was a wonderful recording, Dave.
What band were you with?
I was with the Twins of Dixieland and Harold and Howard Cooper.
The Twins of Dixieland was called?

Harold and Howard Cooper, yes. In fact, I have the rights to that album. It really turned out to be a pretty good album. There was a couple of good players on it. One of which, the drummer had been the drummer for Louis Armstrong's big band. A guy by the name of James Harris, known as Coatesville Harris. And the two Cooper boys played, well, no, I'm sorry. Howard had died and Charlie Borneman was a trombone player. And then Harold, myself, a piano player by the name of Bob King. And a bass player named Junior Williams, who had played with Fats Domino and bands like that.
So we had a good enough man and somehow they managed to get through it.
It worked out right. The guy who did the editing was a whiz with the scissors. And everything turned out pretty good. It's really nothing to be ashamed of.
Yeah, that's incredible. But that's been going on for many years.

Nowadays, you can... I just did an album with Banu Gibson. And my band did about six or seven of the tracks with her. And the rest of the tracks were some material that she had done a few years ago. On one of the tracks, they had an open. And there was just... I don't know if there was anything on it originally between the two vocal choruses. But there was an open chorus with just a piano comping chords and a bass and a drum. And so I went in with the phones and they put me in a booth. And I did a chorus of After You've Gone between her vocals. She did it as a ballad and then played behind her on the last chorus. And I defy anybody to tell you that if they didn't know it. They're just... The engineers just had a way of blending in the presence to where it sounded as if it was all done in the same room.
Yeah, well, they work very hard at that. You can run into some real problems.
Mm-hmm.

We jump about so much, I keep thinking we're going to forget all those early exciting days. We talked about Shockey and some of the people you listen to. You said you knew Joyce did a lot. You can imitate both of them. Were there any other people who stars you were aware of? Louie was mentioned.

Louie was... Let me explain something to you. My first job, first real job with an organized band that I was not the leader on. All these years, in the beginning, I had always been the leader, the prime mover behind these groups. I would go out and get the guys and call the tunes. And the first band that I didn't do all in was the Basin Street Six. George had left the band. And it was a very tight band. It had many arrangements, most of which were head arrangements. I had followed the band for years. I say years, maybe three years. I knew most of the arrangements. So I was really just what they were looking for. Somebody that they didn't have to revamp the whole band for. They just had to teach me a few of the arrangements that I didn't know and kind of polish the burrs down on me. Because I was very young and inexperienced. But I was told to play like George. They wanted me to play George's style. Which was easy enough. It wasn't that difficult. And I was familiar with the way he played. So with the Basin Street Six, I primarily was George Girard. I did all the things that he did. He even sang some of the songs he sang. And some of the newer tunes that we did that I could be a little different on. We did a record date. We discussed it on the Roy Montgomery tune, To Be Remembered. And I backed up Blanche Thomas. And if you listen to it, you can see that Louis was a very big influence on me. Because I kind of played that style behind Blanche. But primarily, I played like George Girard with the Basin Street Six. That's what they wanted. And, you know, the heck.
Yeah, that's how I remember it. Don't think I heard it too much. Where was your blank puppet again?
I first joined them at the Club Slipper on Bourbon Street, which is the 400 block. It was a club that I worked with when I was a kid.
with Jack Teagarden, that's where Jack died. You familiar with the location? It's a plaque out on the wall there now, monstrous plaque, it must be every bit this big. And then we uh...
That's about 4 by 6 inches or something like that.

Then we went out to the Airline Highway at a club, Club Basin Street. How long back? We did. Very short-lived. That was in the last days of the band. Pete left right after we went out there. Roy Zimmerman left right after we went out there. They were replaced by Fano Rupolo on clarinet, and Bobby Brockman on piano. And we played primarily for dancing and some jazz. They were trying to get back to the Lenfence days, when they were primarily a dance band with a couple of Dixieland tunes and a couple of show tunes. But it never did work. Never did work. We really knew nothing about the saloon business. And it just, it's a business you must know very well. If you want any chance at all of winning in it, you have to really know your business. And we knew nothing about it.
You really had to know... You know, it seems very simple sitting on the Asta at a roncel and all you gotta do is buy some liquor and some paper. Seems like it, huh? Yeah. Yeah, that's what you think.

And we had a restaurant there also. Oh, well that's good. Yeah. He knows how to buy food. And, uh, it's amazing. All that stuff is supposed to be dead, but it walks away with the greatest of ease. It develops legs and somehow it gets out of the place. You mean like the... That's exactly what I mean. Yeah, it's, it all disappears. What about the cashier? That's, it's funny how many ways there is a beating of cash register. I just did it. I learned one thing about running a saloon. And that's what I just did. It's not as easy as everybody seems to think.
Yeah. Well, all you gotta do is find an honest bartender. And an honest cashier and honest waiters. And, uh, did anybody drink any of that cashier as a waiters or bartenders?

Oh, I thought you meant the band. No. I, I really don't remember. Uh, I can't remember too many names. All the faces still come up. Uh, the band did some, some pretty, in fact, they were considered some of the, like, world-class drinkers.

But, you hear that bartenders never drink, of course. And I happen to know that's not true. I, I've known a few that drink. Yeah. And, they've heard that all musicians get drunk and drunk. Uh, I've heard that also. Yeah. And, uh, not necessarily shout one way or not. Uh-huh.

Uh, in those days, the Basin Street Six were, I, I was very impressionable. But I can remember, on one intermission at the Slipper, band, band, now I was not much of a drinker in those days. Oh. So that left five real two-handed, two-fisted heavyweight drinkers, went through two-fifths of booze in one thirty minute intermission. Now that's, doing some pretty fancy drinking. Let's see, I think, I don't think any of those guys are alive. Now, let's see, Roy's dead. Johnny Edwards is dead. Joe Rodas is dead. That doesn't, that leaves three of us. Bunny Franks is still alive. Pete, myself, is still alive.
Yeah. And I haven't seen Bunny Franks in years, I haven't.
I've seen him off and on the last couple of years. Still playing on occasion.
Uh-huh.
Whatever happened to the clarinet player? What's his name now? I don't know.

Daniel Raposo. He died. Yeah. Anyway, uh, the, uh, I was always wondering about the salary with the Basin Street Six, how the financial arrangements were, who the lead it was, how the all that arranged things.

It was, uh, I went on the Basin Street Six, and it was a terrific salary at that time. I was making a hundred dollars a week. It's 1953, huh? 52, 53, I guess. When, uh, when, uh, scale, when musicians was only about fifty-eight dollars a week, fifty-six dollars a week. And I was the lowest paid dialing band. I was not one of the, uh, cooperative owners. The rest of the band was, it was a cooperative band. And, uh, it was kind of, uh, how can you say, whoever hollered the loudest got the tone played he wanted. But mostly Joe Rodas handled the mic. After George left the band, Joe handled the microphone. Uh-huh. And, needless to say, the guy with the mic in his hand, if he calls a song, it usually gets played. But, uh, there would be some discussion, sometimes, in, uh, some pretty loud language as to what would be played. But, uh, the continuity was usually pretty good on the band. Uh, I got the job done. It's a good show band. Good show band. And not that bad a Dixie Man band, either.
Well, how did you work the arrangements out? You said, somewhere had?

Well, some more head arrangements. Joe Rodas, uh, was an absolutely wonderful musician. And could write for strings, could write for any combination you wanted. And he did most of the writing. Uh, the dance book was Joe's. stuff had that knack I can remember, we were working at the club slipper at the little bar next door to it which later became the dream bar that you're probably familiar with. They had a piano player in there and the Dukes of Dixieland were doing some syndicated, 15 minute syndicated television shows. They had about a dozen of them to do and Joe Rodas was writing it for them. On his intermission he would sit down in the little bar with either the piano player going or the jukebox going and score these arrangements for the Dukes of Dixieland. Now Harry Shields was a clarinet player on the band and couldn't read. So Joe would have, I believe, I remember him saying, either Joe would teach him the part or one of the Asuntos would teach him the part. And you know, Harry had a wonderful number. But he could, in all that confusion, Joe sat down and wrote a complete television show. All music television show too, not a variety show. It was all music.

Yeah, well, he's one of those people that I heard people talk about. And of course, I always thought of him as a comedian, a clown, who flew around with the trombone and play stuff. And so often I heard him do, he was very, very funny. I'm not belittling him.

He was a good showman. And Joe's biggest trouble was, I guess, in getting any recognition for his playing, was that he didn't play like anybody else. He was a stylist. If you listen to Joe Rodas play, you'd say, hey, that's Joe Rodas. You don't say, hey, that's Joe Rodas. He sounds a little bit like, see, because nobody could put a handle on him. He just, that's the way he played. Very unique player. But he played very well. And he got the, he knew what the trombone player was supposed to do in a band and did it, but his own way.
Nobody paid me into it. He's a clown. To me, he was funnier than Pete or George. I think of them

as being three clowns. Well, Pete was very backward and not very articulate and still isn't. I mean, like, you know, he's got a routine, you know, his little lines that he uses in his show and it comes across very well. But he's not a very articulate person. But Rodas was. Rodas was a very intelligent person. Well read and he spoke French. I mean, like a native, fluently. Yeah. And was familiar with classical literature, both musical and literature, you know. But he
He was very earthy too. Oh, one of the, yeah. Very, very earthy. And behavior and speech, all
of the, yeah. Yeah. Yeah. It's like a live bomb waiting for him to go off. Yeah. And he
had all these contrasting aspects to his character which I think most people missed. Yeah. And

I really didn't know him that well. He was a very warm person. Yeah. Very loving person. Yeah. And and open and giving. He was very generous with himself. Mm-hmm. And taught me an awful lot. And had patience with me. And he did a world of good for me. I watched him drink himself and I didn't see Joe for maybe two years after I moved up to Philadelphia. And he came up there to play with the band for a while. And had just deteriorated to the point where he could not, he just couldn't play anymore. He couldn't get that happy medium between being sober and just the buzz that he wanted. There was no in between. He was either sober or he was uncontrollably drunk. And when he, he was one of those guys that could not play when he had too much to drink. Could not play. Just lost all control. Mm-hmm. Well, I remember him having a heart attack and going in back to hospital. And I guess he came back and played some more after that. Well, the first heart attack he had, yeah, it was a Yeah, it was before I joined the band. Not too, maybe a year or so, I believe. Which would have to be about 1951, 1952. And then I believe he did have another one after that. But after the band had broken up. He was, his health was going on him after that. But the doctors told him he probably would never be active again, much less play. And he just made lives out of him. He went down swinging. He was going to swing at you. But he was grossly overweight. He was one of those kind of guys that would sit down and eat three po' boys and then go looking for something to chase him with. Like a couple dozen hot tamales from manuals on Kalten and Canal. Just a wonderful eater. Yeah, it's a miracle. Yeah, it's a miracle. His stomach didn't fall out. That too, yeah. And liver. And liver. And liver. Yeah. He's a great man.
You said you said you recorded with him. And you got Roy Montgomery's tune to be remembered. And what others were there?

We did Hank Williams' tune, Jambalaya. And My Inspiration, which was a Rodas arrangement, Joe Rodas arrangement. In fact, to be remembered was his arrangement also. And Way Down Yonder and Way Down Yonder and Way Down Yonder and Way Down Yonder and New Orleans. Those were the four songs that were recorded. Now, Way Down Yonder and New Orleans, to my knowledge, has never been released. My inspiration is inserted into an album called Strictly from Dixie, Basin Street 6. And then, to be remembered, in Jambalaya was released as a single. And it is on the jukebox to this day at Mrs. Valente's at the Paddock Lounge. That's the only copy I know of in existence that is still playable. I have a copy on 45 that my daughter, when she was about nine months old, did this to on the floor. It's great to tell.
That hurts. I wonder why you arranged my inspiration.
Pete wanted it. It was one of Pete's features.
I see.

Joe had a way of writing everything very simply. And he had a way of voicing the instruments to where it sounded like more than there really were. Just had that knack. And he did a very good arrangement. It was based pretty closely to the Bob Crosby, my inspiration, the Irving Fazola thing. stuff
Just a few subtle differences.
Was Joe associated with Fazola in any way?
Joe was, Irving Fazola was married to Joe's sister. And I don't know if Joe wrote any for Fazola.
Yeah, I...
I don't really, really don't know.
I don't know what he ever had to do with father's husband and the family relationship.
Yeah, and I think they were probably drinking buddies, too. I don't know if Joe worked with Faz.
Yeah, I never heard anything about him.
At least I know he... I can't remember him ever recording with him.
No, Julian Lane is the one that I remember. That's right.
With those two, the Victor album and the Mercury album. That was Julian Lane.
And I think I saw him in person.
I never saw Faz in person.
One time, one time. You never saw Faz?
Never saw him.
He would have been a little young.

I remember when he died. I remember the sign out in front of the club, down on Canal Boulevard. They put a black wreath around the sign. It was like by the railroad track, by the first railroad track on Canal Boulevard. I forget the name of the club. Was it Tony's? Two Tony's or something like that?
Something like that. Yeah.
Crossed diagonally from Lenfance.
Did you hang around Canal Boulevard that much?
I lived out there.
So you knew what bands were out there, even if you were too young.
Yeah.
And you were that impressed by them, even before you were able to get in the places. Yeah. You'd be underage.

As I said earlier, I was lucky because I was a tall kid. Yeah. And I could get in those places. Sometimes when I was maybe 16 years old, I might be able to get past Tony at Lenfance. If he wasn't looking, I could zip in. See, I'd put one of my daddy's suits on and zip in. Now, every once in a while, Tony would decide that he was the maitre d'. I don't know if you remember Tony. I can't think of his last name. But he would come by and check the bar and spot us and throw us out. Ask us to leave. Tony didn't have to throw you out. He just asked you to leave and you left.
Yeah.
But I was pretty much aware of who was playing out there.
Yeah, I can remember going out to Lenfance a few times. Somehow I didn't get out there very much. It was a long way.
In those days, sure, it was a pretty good way.
I mean, if you had to go to Lenfance, I'd walk to the famous door. You'd go to the famous door in there, sure.
Sure, in those days, you caught the Canal Street streetcar and got off at the cemeteries and you transferred it to a bus.
Now, about 1950, I went to a place across the street from Lenfance. And I can't remember the name of it now.
Across the street?
Yeah, where the base is on Street 6.
Okay, there was a place called Sam Sires. The Starlight Inn. The Starbright Inn. Starlight Inn. On the same side of the railroad track, right? See, there were four places.
Yeah, right close.

Muffins was on the railroad track. They had a place across, on the same side of Canal Boulevard, but across the tracks from Muffins called the Wishing Well. And then across the street from that, on the same side of the tracks, was where Fazola played. And then back on the Lenfance side of the tracks was the Starbright Inn, Sam Sires, Starbright Inn. Which was a hangout for one of them.
And the rockery was where?
The rockery was down on Robert E. Lee in Canal Boulevard.
Yeah, and was that?
That was a drive-in.
No band.
No, it was a drive-in. And they had a, you know, a place inside that didn't seek too many people.

It's funny, you can remember these places and going to them and there was a man called H.J. Boasso who lived back in that neighborhood. Who was in the direct mail advertising business and he played the piano. And you never knew him, I'm sure.
I don't think so.
He would be one of these people that you would never know was a pianist until you went to his shop.
Uh-huh.
He had one of them. And I was just curious about him because he was one of those people that was around.
I'll tell you who lived out there. It was Johnny Ronica.
Yeah.
And H.P. Gently lived out on Canal Boulevard.
You were terribly far from Tony Amarito.
I lived right around the corner from Tony. I lived three doors.
